This page is about two kinds of Tulsa owner: families and entrepreneurs whose business roots go back generations, and newcomers who arrived recently and started something of their own.

Greenwood, then and now

In the early 1920s the Greenwood District north of downtown was home to some 10,000 Black residents and a busy business strip of Black-owned hotels, grocery stores, restaurants, theaters, doctors' and lawyers' offices, two newspapers and a library. It was known nationally as Black Wall Street.

On May 31 and June 1, 1921, a white mob burned about 35 blocks of it, including more than 1,200 homes, its businesses, churches, a school and a hospital. Historians believe as many as 300 people were killed. In June 2021, on the centennial weekend, Greenwood Rising, a history center at the corner of Greenwood and Archer, was dedicated to tell that story in three galleries: before, during and after.

That history is a reason some Tulsa owners care who they hire. Dominion Web Design Pro is Black-owned, and more on that is on our Black-owned web design page. The terms are the same for every customer: free demo, hand-written pages, one-time price.

Tulsa Remote and a wave of new owners

Since late 2018, Tulsa Remote has offered a $10,000 grant, funded by the George Kaiser Family Foundation, to full-time remote workers and self-employed people from elsewhere who move to Tulsa and commit to staying at least a year. Most of the grant is paid out in installments over that year, and members also get coworking space and community events. Thousands of people have moved to Tulsa through the program.

Many newcomers keep their remote jobs. Some start side businesses, consulting practices, studios or shops. They also become customers who do not know which plumber everyone's parents used, so they search. For a long-standing Tulsa business, that is the reason a current website matters: the new neighbor on your block will find you online or not at all.

Name the district, not just the city

Tulsans describe where they are by district, and a site should too. Downtown's Deco District, roughly 1st to 8th Streets between Denver and Cincinnati Avenues, holds Art Deco buildings from the 1920s and 1930s oil boom. The Pearl District leans toward music, cafes and brewpubs. Cherry Street is known for restaurants, boutiques and antiques. Brookside runs along South Peoria Avenue, and Kendall-Whittier has a reputation for makers and murals.

Google says local results depend on relevance, distance and prominence. Saying "a frame shop on Cherry Street" or "HVAC service for midtown and Brookside" helps with the first two in a way that "serving the greater Tulsa area" never will.

Web development in Tulsa: what you probably need, and what you do not

"Web development Tulsa" is a common search, and it often comes from an owner who is not sure what to ask for. Before you hire a web designer in Tulsa or a developer, here is a quick way to sort out which one you need.

Most small businesses need

  • Pages that say what you sell, where and to whom
  • A phone link and a contact form that reaches you
  • Fast loading on a phone
  • Titles, descriptions and a sitemap Google can read
  • Someone to update it when hours or prices change

Custom development is for

  • Customer logins and accounts
  • Online stores with carts and inventory
  • Booking systems built from scratch
  • Connecting to your own business software
  • Apps that do work, not just explain it

We build the first column. If you need the second, hire a developer, and you can still ask us to write the pages around it.

Common questions

What are typical web design rates in Tulsa?

Some designers charge by the hour, some quote a project after a meeting, and some rent you a site by the month. Ours are flat and printed: Starter $497, Pro $997, Agency $1,997, paid once. Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep an AI agent ($297 a month after its free trial), or $49 a month without one. Compare the full first-year cost, not just the build price.

How do I choose between web designers in Tulsa?

Ask each one to show you something built for your business before you pay, to say who writes the words, and to list every monthly charge. Ask who owns the site and the domain when you leave. A designer who answers all four plainly is worth a closer look, whether they are across town or across the state line.

Is web development in Tulsa the same as web design?

People use the words loosely. Design and writing decide what visitors see and read; development is the code and setup underneath, from forms to custom software. Most small businesses need a well-written, fast site with working forms, which is what we build. Custom applications and online stores are not part of our packages.

I just moved to Tulsa to work remotely. Can you build a site for my freelance business?

Yes. A freelancer's site needs a clear statement of what you do and for whom, a few examples of your work, and an easy way to reach you. Starter at $497 is usually enough. You can mention Tulsa or not, depending on whether your clients are local.

Are you based in Tulsa?

No. Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson in Big Sandy, East Texas, and every site is built remotely. Call (903) 636-7511 any hour; an AI receptionist answers and can transfer you to Maurice.
